item.title: She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
item.description:
Work
She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
November 17, 20265:00 AM ET
Andrea Hsu
Ashley Baukman is an apprentice at The Electrical Trades Center in Columbus, Ohio. With the future of work uncertain, some college graduates are turning to the skilled trades for job security.
Andrew Spear for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Andrew Spear for NPR
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.
This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.
For the 36-year-old college graduate and licensed social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.
College didn't deliver
Being the first in her family to graduate from college had been a point of pride for Baukman.

November 16, 20261:04 PM ET
By
Imogen Foulkes
An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29.
Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images
GENEVA — Negotiations on possible rules for the use of lethal autonomous weapons, also known as 'killer robots' are underway at the United Nations in Geneva.
Supporters of controls on autonomous weapons say this week's U.N. conference on Certain Conventional Weapons (or CCW), which meets just once every five years, is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late.
Warfare technology has advanced rapidly in the last few years, with some experts warning that the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and make the decision to kill autonomously.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
item.description:
National
Lindsay Clancy to face a new trial in spring of 2027 over children's killing
November 16, 202611:28 AM ET
By
Bill Chappell
Lindsay Clancy and her attorney Kevin Reddington listen as Judge William Sullivan declares a mistrial at the conclusion of Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Sept. 4.
Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Greg Derr/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
Prosecutors are seeking a new trial for Lindsay Clancy in the deaths of her three children. The trial is scheduled to begin on March 29, 2027.
There had been speculation that the mistrial of her first trial might spur prosecutors to consider lesser charges that wouldn't require a jury, such as manslaughter or second-degree murder. But no changes to the charges were made in Monday's court hearing.
"Given what the charges are, it requires a jury trial," Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Mass.
In response, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington stated, "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."
